scenes.name: Eric B. & Rakim
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Sobrino de la cantante Ruth Brown, Rakim conoció a Eric B. en 1985 por un promotor y grabaron la maqueta en casa de Marley Marl: «My Melody», lenta, y «Eric B. Is President». Su estilo era tan relajado que Shan y Marley se reían de él. Paid in Full (4th & B’way, 1987) retó a todos: el oficio había avanzado. Con «I Know You Got Soul» ayudó a popularizar el sampleo de James Brown. Antes de Rakim casi todos seguían los esquemas de Run-DMC y LL Cool J; él trajo rimas intrincadas, calma absoluta y una fluidez de jazz frente a la «música militar» anterior: para muchos hay Rakim y luego todos los demás. Nas y Jay-Z lo estudiaron.

podcast.title: Performed with Janice Martin (2006)
podcast.body: In 2006, Ruth Brown performed on stage with Janice Martin, singing "Mama He Treat Your Daughter Mean," fulfilling Janice Martin's lifelong ambition. This was their first and only joint performance. "perform on stage with Ruth Brown, singing the song that changed everything for her."

podcast.title: Atlantic Records Success
podcast.body: A former jazz singer, Ruth Brown transitioned into R&B in the 1950s and became instrumental in the growth of Atlantic Records, earning recognition as the woman who helped transform the label into a major force in the music industry. "And Ruth Brown, a former jazz singer who moved into R&B in the 1950s and became known as the woman who helped make Atlantic records into a monster."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Instrumental to Atlantic Records' Success
podcast.body: Ruth Brown, who transitioned from jazz to R&B in the 1950s, became famously known as the woman who was instrumental in transforming Atlantic Records into a major label. Her string of hits significantly boosted the label's profile and financial success during its formative years. "And Ruth Brown, a former jazz singer who moved into R&B in the 1950s and became known as the woman who helped make Atlantic records into a monster."

podcast.title: Lieber & Stoller Collaboration
podcast.body: Ruth Brown was one of the "black performers" whom Jerry Lieber and Mike Stoller admired and recorded with almost exclusively for Atlantic Records. "And at the same time, they were also attached to Atlantic, where they were recording almost exclusively with the black performers that they admired, such as Ruth Brown, LeVern Baker and The Drifters."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Recipient of Lieber's Vocal Direction
podcast.body: Ruth Brown was among the artists whose vocal phrasing was closely directed by Jerry Lieber when Lieber and Stoller produced their records. "When Lieber and Stoller produced an artist, whether it was Elvis or Ruth Brown or the coasters or whoever, they would get them to follow Lieber's phrasing as closely as possible."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Recorded with Atlantic Session Musicians
podcast.body: Ruth Brown was one of the artists who recorded with the standard Atlantic session musicians and arrangers, the same personnel who worked with Ray Charles on his early Atlantic records, indicating a shared musical infrastructure. "The same people who were making records with Ruth Brown or LeVern Baker."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Songs Closer to Jazz than Country
podcast.body: The songs recorded by Ruth Brown, along with LeVern Baker and Dinah Washington, were described as being closer to jazz than to country music, making Janice Martin's performance of them with country instrumentation a unique challenge. "The songs, Brown, Baker and Washington recorded were all closer to jazz than to country music."
